name: GT20029
lead: GT20029 is an investigational topical androgen receptor (AR) degrader developed by Kintor Pharmaceutical of China for androgenetic alopecia (male pattern hair loss) and acne. It is a PROTAC (proteolysis-targeting chimera), a type of molecule that tags a target protein for destruction by the cell's proteasome rather than only blocking it.[1][3] The appearance goal is thicker, denser scalp hair by reducing androgen signalling in the hair follicle, applied to the scalp rather than taken as a pill.

A 2025 review of topical PROTACs names GT20029 and AH-001 as AR degraders in clinical trials for androgenetic alopecia, with the aim of localised degradation and lower systemic exposure.[3] A 2026 expert review of emerging hair-loss therapies lists GT20029 alongside clascoterone among topical androgen-receptor antagonists and degraders, and notes that topical and oral minoxidil, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors and oral antiandrogens remain the mainstay of treatment.[9]

Phase 1 safety trials were completed, and a randomized Phase 2 trial in 180 Chinese men with Hamilton-Norwood III vertex to V alopecia has been published.[4][5][6][7] The drug is not approved anywhere. Forum users have followed its trial news with interest as a possible non-systemic alternative to finasteride-type drugs.
infobox: Phase 2 published; Phase 3 reported by the sponsor [1]

paras: GT20029 is formulated as a gel or solution for application to the scalp, and was also developed for acne vulgaris, another androgen-influenced skin condition.[1][3][5] It comes from Kintor Pharmaceutical, a Suzhou-based company that Grokipedia describes as focused on androgen-receptor signalling in dermatology and oncology; Grokipedia reports that the company's investigational new drug applications were cleared in China and the United States in 2021.[1]

Androgenetic alopecia is described as an age-related, androgen-dependent condition in which dihydrotestosterone and the androgen receptor drive follicular miniaturization.[4][9] Existing options act by lowering DHT (finasteride, dutasteride), stimulating follicles (minoxidil) or blocking androgens systemically. Reviews note widespread patient concern about sexual side effects of oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, which has increased interest in topical and locally acting approaches.[2]

The compound links an androgen receptor binder to a ligase-recruiting group so that AR is ubiquitinated and degraded. Developers describe the goal as reducing androgen signalling in scalp skin while limiting systemic exposure compared with oral 5-alpha reductase inhibitors.[1][3]

PROTACs were first pursued mainly as systemic cancer drugs; AR-targeting PROTACs have been reviewed extensively for castration-resistant prostate cancer.[10] A 2025 Journal of Medicinal Chemistry perspective describes topical use as a way to achieve localised protein degradation while minimizing systemic toxicity, and lists challenges including stability, tissue penetration and selective target engagement under physiological conditions.[3]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports efficacy in a mouse DHT hair-loss model, inhibition of sebaceous gland enlargement in a hamster flank-organ model and low systemic exposure in animals; these claims have not been checked against primary papers.[1]
Two Phase 1 trials (n=92 and n=123) of GT20029 in healthy subjects and people with alopecia or acne were registered as completed.[5][6]

A multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial ran from April 2023 to April 2024. It randomized 180 Chinese men with Hamilton-Norwood IIIv-V alopecia equally into six groups receiving 0.5% or 1.0% GT20029 or placebo, either once daily or twice weekly for 12 weeks.[4][7] The primary endpoint was change in target-area non-vellus hair count at week 12; secondary endpoints included hair count at week 6, hair width and the terminal-to-vellus hair ratio.[4]

All four GT20029 groups showed significant increases in hair count at week 12 (p<0.001). The 0.5% once-daily and 1.0% twice-weekly groups improved significantly over their respective placebo groups (p=0.032 and p=0.023), and hair width improved significantly in the 1.0% twice-weekly group versus placebo (p=0.011). Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar across groups and mostly mild.[4]

A later commentary discusses methodological considerations in evaluating these early outcomes.[8] The trial enrolled Chinese men only, and no head-to-head comparison with finasteride or minoxidil has been published.
Established treatments for male pattern hair loss include oral finasteride and dutasteride and minoxidil; reviews list new mechanism-targeted drugs, including AR degraders, as emerging options.[2][9]
GT20029 is investigational and is not approved by any regulator; it is not available as a regulated product.[1][9]

timeline.event: First Phase 1 study of GT20029 begins.[5]
Phase 2 trial in Chinese men begins.[7]
Phase 2 results published in J Dermatol Treat.[4]
Commentary on early outcomes and expert reviews list GT20029 among emerging hair-loss drugs.[8][9]

lore.intro: GT20029 is discussed on looksmaxxing forums as a pipeline hair-loss drug; no forum posts are cited here.

claims.claim: A topical AR degrader could replace finasteride without systemic side effects
claims.believers: Proponents point to localised AR degradation and low systemic exposure as the advantage.
claims.experts: Reviews describe topical PROTACs as a strategy to localise degradation; long-term safety and efficacy comparisons with finasteride are not yet published. [3][9]

card.summary: An experimental topical AR-degrading PROTAC for male pattern hair loss, with a published Phase 2 trial and no approval.
card.note: Investigational; only early-phase trials, mainly in Chinese men.

quick.overview:
GT20029 is an investigational gel or solution from Kintor Pharmaceutical meant to remove androgen receptors from scalp skin.

A 180-man Phase 2 trial in China has been published; it is not approved anywhere.
quick.mechanism: It is a PROTAC: it marks the androgen receptor for destruction by the proteasome, aiming to act locally.
quick.risks: Phase 1 and 2 safety data exist but detailed long-term data do not. It is unavailable as a regulated product.

chain: Applied to the scalp as a gel or solution
Degrades androgen receptors in scalp skin
Possible increase in hair count and width
angle.text: GT20029 is designed to reduce androgen-driven follicle miniaturization locally, so that hair on the crown and vertex becomes denser. Published human data come from early-phase trials.
